fixes.explanation: That's him, baker. Judah goes out in front of the family, and Joseph is the one he heads to for directions to Goshen (Genesis 46:28). Jacob has one of his sons go first and find the way. I'd make a terrible scout, since I can get turned around between the oven and the counter.

Reuben is a fair thought, since he's the first name in the list, Jacob's firstborn (Genesis 46:8). But the son who goes in front is Judah. Judah is the one who goes to Joseph for directions to Goshen.

Benjamin is a natural pick, since he's one of the two sons born to Rachel, same as Joseph (Genesis 46:19). Still, the son Jacob sends in front is Judah. Judah is the one who goes to Joseph for directions to Goshen. Benjamin isn't named for that job.

Yes, baker. Joseph brings in his father Jacob and presents him before Pharaoh, Egypt's king, and Jacob blesses him. Then in verse 10 the text says Jacob blessed Pharaoh again before he departed. Two blessings in one visit. That's a guest who leaves a room better than he found it.

That's it, baker. At Beersheba he offers sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac. The text puts those sacrifices right there on the way out of Canaan. I'd have stopped to check whether I left the oven on, so I'm glad this stop was about God.

Big thinking, but that's not what God says. He says, “I will go down with you to Egypt, and I will surely bring you back.” He also says He will make Jacob into a great nation there. Nothing in the vision gives Egypt to Jacob. The promise is that God goes with him and brings him back.

I get the thought, since moving a big family is a lot to carry. But the text says, “They also took the livestock and possessions they had acquired in the land of Canaan…” So the livestock goes down to Egypt too. Nobody in that family is leaving the animals behind.

Yes, baker. Joseph prepared his chariot and went to meet his father, and then he presented himself to him, embraced him, and wept profusely. He doesn't stay up in the chariot. I think that's a whole lot of feeling in one meeting.

That's it. Israel says, “Finally I can die, now that I have seen your face and know that you are still alive!” His reason is right there in his own words: he has seen Joseph's face, and he knows Joseph is alive. I think that moment hits him all at once.

It's actually true, friend. Joseph tells his brothers what to say when Pharaoh asks about their occupation: “Your servants have raised livestock ever since our youth…” He adds that their fathers did too. So the statement on the card matches what the text says. It's also just who they are.

That's a fair guess, but Joseph never brings up who owns the land. His reason is in verse 34: “…since all shepherds are detestable to the Egyptians.” The whole reason comes down to how the Egyptians feel about shepherds. I do love checking paperwork, being a stamper, but there's none in this answer.

That's right. They tell Pharaoh, “…there is no pasture for the flocks of your servants, since the famine in the land of Canaan has been severe.” Flocks are what they raise, and the famine is the reason they give. They keep it plain and don't dress it up.

That would make a dramatic story, but it isn't what they say. They tell Pharaoh there is no pasture for their flocks, since the famine in the land of Canaan has been severe. No enemies come up anywhere in their answer. The reason they give is the famine.

Yes, baker. Pharaoh says, “And if you know of any talented men among them, put them in charge of my own livestock.” Notice it starts with “if.” It's an offer, and Pharaoh doesn't say such men are there. He just says what the job would be.

Storehouses is a thought, since earlier in Genesis Joseph is the one who gathers up the food (Genesis 41:48). But Pharaoh's offer is, “And if you know of any talented men among them, put them in charge of my own livestock.” He says “if,” so he isn't saying such men exist. What he names is his livestock.

Chariots are flashy, I'll admit. But Pharaoh says, “…put them in charge of my own livestock.” Just before that, the brothers told him they are shepherds, both they and their fathers. Livestock is the job Pharaoh names.

That's a big number, and it's a real one in Genesis. Abraham lived a hundred and seventy-five years (Genesis 25:7). But Jacob says, “My travels have lasted 130 years…” That's Jacob's own number, and it's lower.
